lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: describe the structure of the leaf and explain how it is adapted for photosynthesis

primer.text: You know leaves are a plant's food factories, and you have met photosynthesis's inputs and outputs. This lesson opens the factory floor: each tissue layer of the leaf, what it does, and how the whole stacked design — from waxy cuticle to stomata — turns the leaf into an efficient photosynthesising machine.

modules.title: Leaf Layers and Their Adaptations
modules.opening: A leaf is built in layers, each pulling its weight. The waxy cuticle and epidermis protect without blocking light, the packed palisade mesophyll catches the most sun, the spongy mesophyll circulates air for gas exchange, and the stomata and veins handle entry, exit and delivery — every structure pointing at photosynthesis.
keyPoints: The wax cuticle protects the leaf on both sides while preventing water loss.
The upper epidermis is thin and transparent, letting light reach the palisade layer.
Palisade mesophyll cells are column-shaped and packed with chloroplasts for maximum absorption.
Spongy mesophyll holds air spaces that raise the surface area for gas diffusion.
Guard cells open and close the stomata to admit carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
Xylem delivers water and phloem carries sucrose and amino acids to and from the leaf.

low.restatement: Protect, catch light, exchange gases, deliver supplies: the four jobs of the layers.
low.analogy: A greenhouse: glass roof, sun-catching plants, vents and a water line.
low.examPointer: Reproduce the structures table row by row; each structure-function pair is a mark.

medium.restatement: The layering is a trade-off solved in order: protection first, light capture next, gas logistics underneath.
medium.analogy: A well-run shopfront: window, display, storeroom and loading bay.
medium.examPointer: Link each adaptation explicitly to photosynthesis when asked why.

glossary.definition: The chloroplast-packed column-cell layer that catches most incoming light.
Pores, mostly on the leaf underside, where gas exchange and water evaporation occur.
The xylem-and-phloem strand that transports substances to and from the leaf.
